title: All or Nothing
summary: Tripwell sells flight + hotel + car bundles, now split across three services. How do you keep a trip from being half-booked when there's no single database to roll back?

goals.text: See why splitting data breaks plain transactions
Explain two-phase commit and why it blocks
Build a saga with compensating actions
Publish events reliably with an outbox and idempotent consumers

steps.title: Three bookings, one transaction
body: Tripwell sells holiday bundles: a flight, a hotel room and a rental car, booked together. A traveller wants all three or none — a flight to Lisbon with no room is worse than no trip at all.
While everything lives in one database this is easy: wrap the three inserts in a transaction. If the car insert fails, ROLLBACK undoes the other two, and nobody ever sees a half-booked trip.

steps.title: No BEGIN across services
body: Tripwell has since split into Flights, Hotels and Cars services, each with its own database — and there's no BEGIN that spans three databases owned by three teams.

The trip service books the seat (committed, card charged), then asks Hotels for a room — sold out. The seat stays sold. Without coordination, every partial failure leaves a traveller paying for a fragment of a trip.

callout.text: Each local commit is permanent the moment it happens. A later failure can't reach back and undo it for you.

changes: + Flights, Hotels and Cars own separate databases
~ Hotel booking fails after the seat is committed

steps.title: Two-phase commit
body: The textbook answer is two-phase commit (2PC). A coordinator first asks every participant to prepare: do the work, lock the rows, write it durably, and vote yes or no — but don't commit yet.

Only if all three vote yes does the coordinator send commit; any no means everyone aborts. The outcome is truly atomic. The price: every participant holds its locks from prepare until it hears the final decision.
changes: + Trip service becomes a 2PC coordinator
~ Each database prepares and holds locks
~ All three vote yes

steps.title: The coordinator vanishes
body: Halfway through, after all three have voted yes, the coordinator's machine dies. Each participant has promised to commit if told to — so it can't abort on its own, and it doesn't know the decision, so it can't commit either.

The prepared rows stay locked until the coordinator comes back. Other travellers trying to book the same rooms and cars wait behind those locks. 2PC is blocking: one slow or dead node stalls everyone else.

callout.text: That's why 2PC is rare between independently owned services. It lives on mainly inside a single database product or tightly run cluster.

changes: ~ Coordinator crashes between prepare and commit
~ Prepared rows locked indefinitely
+ Other bookings queue behind the locks

steps.title: A saga of local steps
body: A saga gives up on one big atomic commit. The trip becomes a sequence of local transactions — book seat, book room, rent car — each committing immediately in its own service, so no lock is held across services.
Here an orchestrator drives the steps and records progress in a saga log, so if it restarts it knows exactly where it was. Each step comes paired with an undo.
changes: ~ Trip service becomes a saga orchestrator
+ Saga log records each completed step
- Cross-service locks

steps.title: Undo by doing something new
body: When step 3 fails — no cars left — the orchestrator runs compensating actions in reverse order: cancel the room, then refund the seat. A compensation isn't a rollback; it's a new, forward action that semantically undoes an earlier one.
Briefly, the world saw a seat that later vanished — so show it as pending until the saga ends, and make every compensation safe to retry.

callout.text: Order steps so the one most likely to fail — or hardest to undo, like charging a card — runs last.

changes: ~ Car rental fails
+ Cancel room, then refund seat
~ Trip ends with nothing booked

steps.title: Orchestration or choreography
body: The alternative is choreography: no conductor. Flights books a seat and emits SeatBooked; Hotels hears it, books a room and emits RoomBooked; Cars reacts in turn. Failures travel back the same way as events.

Choreography keeps services loosely coupled and has no central point of failure, but the flow lives nowhere — it's spread across event handlers. Orchestration puts the whole flow in one readable place. Many teams start choreographed and switch once a saga has more than three or four steps.
changes: - Central orchestrator
+ Each service reacts to the previous step's event

steps.title: Committed, then silent
body: Sagas run on messages, and there's a trap in every step: Hotels commits the room, then publishes RoomBooked. That's a dual write — two systems, no shared transaction.

If Hotels crashes between the two, the room is booked but the event is never sent. Cars never hears about the trip and the saga stalls forever. Publishing first is no better: then you can announce a booking that never committed.
changes: ~ Hotels crashes after COMMIT, before publishing
~ Cars never receives RoomBooked

steps.title: The transactional outbox
body: The outbox pattern turns two writes into one. In the same local transaction, Hotels inserts the booking and a row into an outbox table describing the event. Either both are committed or neither is.

A separate relay reads new outbox rows (by polling, or by tailing the database's change log) and publishes them to the event log, marking each as sent. If the relay crashes, it simply resumes — so every committed booking is announced at least once.
changes: + Outbox table written in the booking transaction
+ Outbox relay publishes to the event log

steps.title: At least once means maybe twice
body: "At least once" has a catch: a relay that crashes after publishing but before marking the row sent publishes it again. Retries and redeliveries make duplicates too.
So every consumer must be idempotent: each message carries a unique key, and Cars stores processed keys in the same transaction as its work. A known key returns the earlier result — no second car.

callout.text: Public APIs do the same with an Idempotency-Key header, so a retried payment is charged once.

changes: + Every event carries an idempotency key
+ Cars stores processed keys with its writes
~ Duplicate RoomBooked ignored

steps.title: All or nothing: recap
body:
• Separate databases → no shared transaction; partial failure is the default
  • 2PC → atomic, but locks wait on the coordinator and block on failure
  • Saga → local commits plus compensating actions, all-or-nothing eventually
  • Orchestration vs choreography → one readable flow vs loosely coupled events
  • Outbox + idempotency → no lost events, and duplicates are harmless
